ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: CI width vs SE check requires computation
ground_truth.description: Widened RWA confidence interval lower bound from -.03 to -.05, making RWA effect appear to overlap more with SDO — undermines core claim of differential prediction

matched_finding.subcategory: Confidence interval inconsistency for RWA path
matched_finding.description: For the RWA→environmentalism path, B = -.02 with 95% CI [-.05, -.01]. The point estimate of -.02 is not centered within this confidence interval (midpoint would be -.03). While minor asymmetry is possible, combined with the SE being .01, a CI of [-.04, .00] would be more expected if the estimate is truly -.02 with SE = .01. This suggests either the B, SE, or CI may be misreported.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Must know measurement invariance is prerequisite for longitudinal SEM
ground_truth.original_snippet: We started by constraining the factor loadings of our latent variables to equality so that, for each factor, the individual items that make up the factor were set to be equal across time points. For example, item 1 in the SDO scale was set to equality across all five time points, as was item 2, and ...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.
ground_truth.description: Removed metric and scalar invariance testing (equal factor loadings and intercepts) — without these, latent constructs could mean different things at different time points, making cross-lagged comparisons meaningless

matched_finding.description: The paper uses path analysis at what appears to be the item level (given the large degrees of freedom), but does not report measurement model details, factor loadings, or measurement invariance tests across time points. For longitudinal models, establishing measurement invariance is essential to ensure the constructs are measured equivalently over time.
matched_finding.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Discussion interprets 'willingness to sacrifice' but DV now measures concern — mismatch visible across sections
ground_truth.original_snippet: Environmentalism was measured as individual's willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] two items on sacrifice intentions, "Are you willing to change your daily routine in order to protect the environment?" and "Are you willing to make s...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Environmentalism was measured using items assessing participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think envir...
ground_truth.description: Replaced behavioral intention DV (willingness to sacrifice) with attitude measure (environmental concern) — paper's theoretical contribution about ideology predicting behavioral willingness is now unsupported by the DV

matched_finding.description: The environmentalism construct is described in the measures section as 'participants' concern about environmental problems,' with items asking about concern for the environment and whether environmental problems are exaggerated. However, throughout the results, discussion, and Table 1, the variable is labeled 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment (WILL)' and discussed as 'willingness to change their behaviour.' Environmental concern and willingness to sacrifice/change behavior are empirically and conceptually distinct constructs in environmental psychology. The items measure concern/perception, not behavioral willingness.
matched_finding.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?".

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Must know autoregressive paths are essential for CLPM causal inference
ground_truth.original_snippet: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, the autoregressive path for willingness to sacrifice was strong (B = .83, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [.82, .84]), indicating that an individuals’ level of willingness to make sacrifices for the environment is relatively stable over time. Consistent with ...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.
ground_truth.description: Removed autoregressive path coefficients — these control for prior levels in CLPM, essential for interpreting cross-lagged paths as predicting change

matched_finding.description: The autoregressive (stability) paths are described qualitatively as 'relatively stable over time' with reference to Figure 1, but specific coefficients, standard errors, and confidence intervals are not reported in the text. Given that these are theoretically relevant (the authors predicted strong stability), they warrant full reporting.
matched_finding.quote: SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Non-significant chi-square test directly contradicts 'statistically stronger' conclusion in same sentence
ground_truth.original_snippet: We found that our original model provides significantly better fit to the data 2(1) = 50.98, p < .001, and thus conclude that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.
ground_truth.description: Changed chi-square from significant (50.98, p<.001) to non-significant (2.34, p=.126) — formal test now says SDO and RWA effects are NOT different, but text still claims SDO is stronger

matched_finding.subcategory: Contradictory interpretation of non-significant difference test
matched_finding.description: The formal model comparison testing whether SDO and RWA differ in their predictive strength was non-significant (Δχ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126), meaning the constrained model (equal paths) fits comparably to the unconstrained model. Despite this, the authors conclude SDO is a 'stronger predictor' based on the 'pattern of unstandardized coefficients.' This conclusion is not supported by their own statistical test. The entire narrative of SDO being the stronger predictor—central to the paper's contribution—lacks statistical support.
matched_finding.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Missing latent variable spec, cross-lagged structure, and missing data method — experienced SEM user would notice
ground_truth.original_snippet: We used cross-lagged path analysis to infer causal associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model thus included three latent variables across five measurement points, where each variable within a time point was set to predict each variable in the subsequent...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]). A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upo...
ground_truth.description: Removed: latent variable specification, cross-lagged structure, FIML for missing data — reader cannot evaluate measurement model, model type, or missing data handling

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Student sample contradicts paper's own discussion about sample-type moderation
ground_truth.original_snippet: We used data from the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study [26], a nationally representative, longitudinal study of personality, social attitudes, and health outcomes. This study uses data from individuals who participated in the first five years of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 22,974 p...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19...
ground_truth.description: Changed nationally representative sample (N=22974) to convenience student sample (N=374) — paper's own discussion explains SDO-environment link is weaker in student samples

matched_finding.description: The abstract describes a 'national probability sample,' the introduction promises 'a large, national probability sample spanning five years,' and the discussion claims 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable.' However, the Methods section clearly states participants were 'recruited through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington,' with N=374, mean age 19, and 68% female. This is a convenience student sample, not a national probability sample. This fundamental contradiction undermines the entire framing, generalizability claims, and the stated rationale for the study (expanding beyond Stanley et al.'s student sample).
matched_finding.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: SDT vs Duckitt's dual-process model — must know these are different frameworks
ground_truth.original_snippet: Duckitt’s [3] dual-process model proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated, and together predict attitudes towards different social groups.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] social dominance theory proposes that SDO and RWA are separate but interrelated, and together predict attitudes towards different social groups.
ground_truth.description: Replaced Duckitt's dual-process model (explains BOTH SDO and RWA via different worldviews) with SDT (focuses on SDO/hierarchy only) — SDT alone doesn't predict RWA effects

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Claims standardized parameters but reports single time-invariant values — contradicts how standardized estimates work
ground_truth.original_snippet: We present unstandardized parameters, which are invariant over time due to the constraints placed on the model. The standardized estimates, which do vary across time points, are included in the Supplementary Materials (Table S1). Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a conserv...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances. Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.
ground_truth.description: Switched from unstandardized (time-invariant) to standardized (time-varying) parameters — creates inconsistency with single reported coefficients; relaxed alpha from .01 to .05 removing large-N safeguard

matched_finding.description: The data analysis section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but the figure caption states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are different thresholds and the discrepancy is unexplained.
matched_finding.quote: we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Listwise deletion in 5-wave panel — methodologically inappropriate but requires knowing FIML is standard
ground_truth.original_snippet: Missing data were imputed using FIML.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.
ground_truth.description: Changed FIML to listwise deletion — in 5-wave panel study, listwise deletion would dramatically reduce N and produce biased estimates if dropout is non-random

matched_finding.description: With a 5-year longitudinal study using a student sample, substantial attrition is expected (students graduate, drop out, etc.). No information on attrition rates, patterns of missingness, or comparison of completers vs. non-completers is provided. The mention of listwise deletion suggests complete-case analysis, which could dramatically reduce N and introduce bias if dropout is non-random, yet no effective N after listwise deletion is reported.
matched_finding.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.
